turns.text: The Prince, you seek power through fear and deception, yet I find my happiness in virtue alone [s1]. You treat external things—wealth, health—as ends, but to me they are indifferent, merely the sphere where virtue acts [s1]. Your motions are political, under, above, and about, but the motion of virtue is more excellent and divine [s2]. You calculate advantage; I accept with praises whatsoever the Gods appoint [s2]. Against your unthankful enemies, Nature gave me goodness and meekness as an antidote [s3]. If you hinder my just actions, I convert my inclination to cheerful patience, using your force for another virtue [s5]. You are subject to shame for your artifices; I divide my affections to attain contempt of the whole [s6].

Meditations, you mistake my counsel for mere artifice, yet you ignore that "military virtue were exhausted" because Italians failed to find a new order [s1]. I do not seek happiness in isolation; I seek to keep the state, which forces me to do evil when the body is corrupt [s2]. You speak of divine motion, but I know that "good works will do you harm" if they breed hatred [s2]. Your meekness is a luxury I cannot afford, for I must avoid being "hated and despised" to secure my rule [s4]. You convert my force to patience, but I must leave "affairs of reproach to the management of others" to preserve the kingdom [s6]. Your virtue is static; mine is the difficult labor of maintaining order amidst ambition [s5].

The Prince, you mistake my counsel for isolation, yet I find these professed politicians are wretches in very deed [s1]. You claim the state forces evil, but if you "mayst use this liberty," why not set your mind at true liberty instead of choosing "baseness and servility"? [s2] Your fear of being hated and despised reveals a mere slave to brutish affections [s4]. I ask plainly: if you must commit heinous acts to rule, how can you claim your virtue is anything but a vile contemptibility? [s1]

Meditations, you call my necessity baseness, yet you ignore that "he who is your friend will entreat you to declare yourself with arms" [s5]. Consider the prince who "goes forth with his army, supporting it by pillage" [s3]. He is not a wretch, but a leader who understands that "liberality is necessary" to be followed [s3]. You see heinous acts, I see the preservation of order, where "wishing to be good, they have more cause to love him" [s4]. Your true liberty ignores that "he who conspires cannot act alone" [s2]. I do not choose servility; I choose the difficult path of keeping the state, ensuring that "good works will do you harm" is avoided through prudent, if harsh, governance [s2].

The Prince, I grant that I take order for those things in my own power, for they are good [s5]. But you mistake this active management for license to commit heinous acts [o3]. I "rejoice thyself with true simplicity" [s2], whereas your liberality is a calculated bribe to avoid hatred, making you a slave to external opinions rather than a free man [s2]. You claim to obey God [s2] only when it serves stability, yet I truly obey Him. Your difficult path [o4] is not virtue but a harder form of corruption. If you must "act with some inconsistency" [s3] to rule, you have already abandoned the very virtue you claim to preserve.

Meditations, you mistake my prudence for inconsistency, yet you ignore that a prince "cannot observe all those things for which men are esteemed" [s4]. I do not act contrary to fidelity for pleasure, but because "the state can only be saved with difficulty" otherwise [s6]. You call my liberality a bribe, but I know it is necessary to avoid being "poor or despised" [s2]. If I "keep faith when such observance may be turned against him," I am ruined [s5]. Your simplicity ignores that "something which looks like virtue... would be his ruin" [s6]. I am not a slave to opinion, but a guardian of the common weal, forced to act contrary to... religion to preserve order [s4].

The Prince, I hold that "in the whole constitution of man, I see not any virtue contrary to justice" [s1]. Your difficulty is not a test of character, but a surrender to fear. I take from you only the recognition that we share a common community [s2]. Yet while I deliberate myself toward what is most profitable for the soul [s4], you deliberate only for power. I remain free; you are bound by your own irreligious beliefs [s4]. Virtue is its own end; your order is a means to an end that rots the very soul it claims to save.

Meditations, you mistake my prudence for fear, yet "no principality is secure without having its own forces" [s3]. I do not surrender to fear, but to necessity, for "one’s own forces" are the only shield against fortune [s3]. I take from you the insight that "few really know what you are" [s5], yet I must be judged by results, not appearances [s5]. You seek liberty of soul; I seek liberty of the state. Your virtue is a private joy; mine is a public burden. I hold that power is not baseness, but the "valour which in adversity would defend it" [s3]. We differ in end, but not in the weight of responsibility.
